native_result.query: What kind of demographic disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated?
native_result.HypoA: Gender disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated, with males having higher median wealth than females.
native_result.HypoB: Among NLSY79 young adults, those who were subsequently incarcerated (ever_jailed=1, jailed at some point between 1985 and 1994) already held sharply lower wealth in 1985 than those never jailed, and this 1985 baseline disadvantage was patterned by both sex and race. Overall, ever-incarcerated individuals had a median 1985 composite wealth of about $720 versus $3,600 for the never-jailed (difference -$2,880; bootstrap 95% CI [-3,600, -2,300]; 0.20x, i.e. roughly 80% lower; Mann-Whitney p=1.6e-10). The pattern is concentrated in men, who account for 252 of the 289 ever-jailed: among men the median was $1,000 versus $4,000 (difference -$3,000, 95% CI [-3,800, -2,470], ratio 0.25, p=4.3e-09). Within ever-incarcerated men there is a clear racial gradient in starting wealth - white men $2,000, black men $800 (0.40x white), hipanic (Hispanic) men $700 (0.35x white). Comparing jailed against non-jailed within the same race and sex, the largest relative penalty falls on Hispanic men (median -$4,300; 0.14x their non-jailed peers; p=0.00012), then white men (-$3,500; 0.36x; p=0.029); for black men the within-group difference is small (-$700; 0.53x; p=0.082, CI including 0) not because disadvantage is absent but because non-jailed black men were themselves already near the bottom (median $1,500), a compressed floor. Ever-jailed women are too few (n=37; cells of 9, 12 and 16, all n<30, two with a median of exactly 0 so ratios are undefined) to assess incarceration gradients within women, and those figures are descriptive only. Robustness: excluding negative/zero wealth leaves conclusions unchanged (ALL $1,000 vs $4,300, 0.23x), and in relative terms so does removing duplicated rows (0.20x vs 0.23x); however, the duplicated rows are systematically the poorest (their own median 1985 wealth is $0 vs $6,000), so absolute dollar levels are not stable while relative comparisons and directions are. As a trend reference only (nominal dollars, unknown component mix, hence not real-wealth change), the gap had not narrowed by 1990 (jailed $0 vs $10,500) or 1996 ($0 vs $8,500). Because ever_jailed spans 1985-1994 while wealth is measured in 1985, this is a forward-looking group difference - people later incarcerated were already at the bottom of the 1985 wealth distribution, most acutely Hispanic and black men - and must not be read as a causal effect of incarceration.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Profiled data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (n=12,013; no missing values; race white/black/'hipanic' as spelled in source; ever_jailed prevalence 2.4%). 2) Main analysis (duplicates kept per researcher; negative and zero composite_wealth kept; unweighted sample medians) over the 3x2x2 race x sex x ever_jailed grid reporting median, n, Q1/Q3/IQR and 2,000-replicate percentile bootstrap CIs of each median (numpy default_rng, seed=20261022). 3) Gap quantities: jailed-minus-non-jailed median difference per race x sex cell plus ratio where both medians > 0 (flagged 'not computable' when a median <= 0), with bootstrap CIs for differences/ratios and two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests on full wealth distributions. 4) Binary ever_jailed summaries for the whole sample and for males only (n=252 jailed) as the inferential layer; female cells (n=9/12/16) descriptive only. 5) Robustness: de-duplicated sample (n=10,114) with per-cell percentage differences and a duplicate-structure diagnostic; appendix sensitivity restricted to wealth >= 0. 6) 1990/1996 medians by incarceration status as trend reference only, explicitly not interpreted as real wealth change. Scripts: analysis/nls_1985_wealth_analysis.py, analysis/robustness_gap_inference.py; outputs analysis/results_tables.txt, analysis/gap_inference.txt, analysis/FINDINGS.md.

sub_hypo.text: Gender disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated, with males having higher median wealth than females.
sub_hypo.context: Individuals in the National Longitudinal Study of Youth's 1979 cohort who were jailed between 1985 and 1994 (ever_jailed = 1).
sub_hypo.relations: Among ever-incarcerated individuals, males have higher median wealth in 1985 than females.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Gender disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated, with males having higher median wealth than females.

sub_hypo.text: NLSY79 young adults jailed at some point between 1985 and 1994 already had substantially lower median composite wealth in 1985 than those never jailed: approximately $720 versus $3,600.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 sample of 12,013 respondents; main analysis uses unweighted medians, retaining duplicates and negative or zero wealth. Incarceration status covers 1985–1994, so this is a forward-looking group comparison, not a causal effect of incarceration.
sub_hypo.relations: Ever-jailed minus never-jailed median wealth difference is -$2,880 (bootstrap 95% CI [-$3,600, -$2,300]); median ratio 0.20, approximately 80% lower; two-sided Mann–Whitney p=1.6e-10.

sub_hypo.text: The baseline wealth disadvantage is concentrated in men, who comprise 252 of the 289 ever-jailed respondents; ever-jailed men had median 1985 wealth of $1,000 versus $4,000 for never-jailed men.
sub_hypo.context: Male respondents in the NLSY79 sample; incarceration defined as any jailing during 1985–1994; unweighted analysis retaining duplicates and nonpositive wealth.
sub_hypo.relations: Among men, the jailed-minus-never-jailed median difference is -$3,000 (95% CI [-$3,800, -$2,470]); median ratio 0.25; Mann–Whitney p=4.3e-09.

sub_hypo.text: Among ever-incarcerated men, 1985 starting wealth follows a racial gradient: white men had median wealth of $2,000, black men $800, and Hispanic men $700.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 male respondents with ever_jailed=1; Hispanic is spelled 'hipanic' in the source data.
sub_hypo.relations: Median wealth is highest for white men, followed by black and Hispanic men; black men's median is 0.40 times white men's, and Hispanic men's is 0.35 times white men's.

sub_hypo.text: Within male race groups, the largest relative baseline wealth disadvantage associated with later incarceration occurs among Hispanic men, followed by white men.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 men compared by 1985–1994 incarceration status within Hispanic and white race groups.
sub_hypo.relations: Hispanic men have a jailed-minus-never-jailed median difference of -$4,300 and median ratio 0.14 (p=0.00012); white men have a difference of -$3,500 and ratio 0.36 (p=0.029).

sub_hypo.text: Among black men, the within-group incarceration-associated baseline wealth difference is small because never-jailed black men also had very low wealth, with a median of $1,500.
sub_hypo.context: Black male respondents in the NLSY79 sample, comparing those jailed during 1985–1994 with those never jailed.
sub_hypo.relations: Ever-jailed black men have median wealth $700 below never-jailed black men, with a median ratio of 0.53; p=0.082 and the difference CI includes zero. The small absolute gap reflects a compressed low-wealth floor rather than absence of disadvantage.

sub_hypo.text: Ever-jailed women are too few to assess incarceration-related wealth gradients within women; their race-specific wealth figures are descriptive only.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 ever-jailed women: 37 total, with race-specific cells of 9, 12, and 16, all below 30.
sub_hypo.relations: No inferential incarceration gradient is established for women. Two ever-jailed female race cells have median wealth exactly zero, making median ratios undefined under the analysis rule requiring both medians to be positive.

sub_hypo.text: The direction and relative magnitude of the 1985 incarceration-associated wealth disadvantage persist under wealth-value restrictions and removal of duplicate rows, although absolute dollar levels are not stable.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 robustness analyses: the hypothesis reports excluding negative and zero wealth; the workflow also specifies an appendix restriction to wealth >= 0. Deduplication reduces the sample from 12,013 to 10,114.
sub_hypo.relations: After excluding nonpositive wealth, overall ever-jailed versus never-jailed medians are $1,000 versus $4,300, ratio 0.23. Original versus deduplicated relative comparisons are 0.20 versus 0.23. Duplicated rows are systematically poorer, with median wealth $0 versus $6,000, so absolute levels change while relative comparisons and directions persist.

sub_hypo.text: As a nominal-dollar trend reference, the incarceration-status wealth gap had not narrowed by 1990 or 1996.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 respondents grouped by any jailing during 1985–1994; later wealth comparisons are descriptive trend references only because dollars are nominal and the component mix is unknown.
sub_hypo.relations: Ever-jailed versus never-jailed median wealth is $0 versus $10,500 in 1990 and $0 versus $8,500 in 1996, compared with $720 versus $3,600 in 1985. These comparisons do not establish real-wealth change or causal effects of incarceration.
